standard.title: Commemoration, Anzac Legend and Historical Interpretations
standard.description: the commemoration of the First World War, including different historical interpretations and debates about the nature and significance of the Anzac legend and the war
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify that historical interpretations differ and explain why (AC9HH8K06, AC9HH8K11). They have studied the Gallipoli campaign, the Western Front experience, and the effects of the war on Australian society (AC9HH9K09, AC9HH9K11). They have not yet examined what the 'Anzac legend' claims as a set of values and ideals, how commemoration functions as a cultural practice, or how historians have debated and contested the legend's nature and significance over time.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate the ideals associated with the Anzac tradition and how and why WW1 is commemorated in Australian society; discuss similarities and differences in historians' views of the Anzac legend over time; identify differences between commemoration and glorification; and evaluate the fairness of post-war treaties on the defeated powers, including the Treaty of Versailles on Germany.

nodes.label: The Anzac legend — what it claims and what values it asserts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the Anzac legend as a set of specific values and ideals — mateship, courage, larrikinism, egalitarianism, endurance — and explain where these ideals came from and what they claim about Australian national character.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify the core ideals associated with the Anzac legend (mateship, courage, endurance under adversity, egalitarian disregard for rank, larrikinism), describe where each ideal came from — the Gallipoli and Western Front experience as interpreted by C.E.W. Bean and others — and explain what the legend claims about what it means to be Australian.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the Anzac legend's specific components; trace the legend's origins in C.E.W. Bean's reporting and official histories; explain how the legend was constructed from selective elements of the actual experience (not all soldiers displayed these virtues; the legend emphasises some experiences and omits others); explain what purposes the legend served — national identity, meaning-making for grief, connection to a founding national story; examine how the legend positions Gallipoli as the 'birth' of the Australian nation.
wider: Examine specific texts that constructed the legend — Bean's dispatches, early ANZAC Day speeches, war poetry and art — and analyse the choices made in how soldiers and their experience were represented
Investigate who was excluded from the original legend — First Nations soldiers, women, non-Anglo Australians — and what that exclusion reveals about whose story the legend was originally telling
nodes.hinge_reason: The Anzac legend's content must be understood before its historiographical debate (N3) can proceed. Students who cannot describe what the legend actually claims cannot meaningfully compare historians' views about its nature and significance — they will discuss the debate without knowing what is being debated.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Examining the exclusions from the original legend — and comparing the original to later, more inclusive versions — generates genuine analytical depth about how national narratives are constructed and whose experience they represent. This connects directly to the commemoration vs glorification distinction in N2.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat the Anzac legend as self-evidently true — the actual soldiers were exactly as described — rather than as a specific historical construction that emphasised some elements and omitted others. Making the legend's constructedness explicit is the scaffold for the interpretive debate that follows.

Examining how the legend was constructed from specific sources — Bean's journalism, specific speeches, specific images — and what each source emphasised, builds a more complex understanding than treating the legend as a single, unified thing.

success_criteria: Describes the core ideals of the Anzac legend with at least three examples
Explains where the legend came from and what it claims about Australian national character

nodes.label: Commemoration — how and why WW1 is remembered
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how the First World War is commemorated in Australian society and explain the purposes that commemoration serves — including the distinction between commemoration and glorification.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe the main forms of WW1 commemoration in Australia (ANZAC Day, memorials, the Last Post, the minute of silence, Dawn Services), explain at least two purposes commemoration serves (honouring the dead, maintaining national memory, community gathering, educating future generations), and identify the distinction between commemorating sacrifice and glorifying war.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the evolution of ANZAC Day from a solemn memorial day to a major national event — changes in scale, participation, and meaning over time; examine the different ways commemoration is practiced (Dawn Services, school ceremonies, sporting tributes, pilgrimages to Gallipoli); explain who participates and why; examine the distinction between commemoration as respectful remembrance of sacrifice vs glorification as celebrating war as heroic and desirable; explain why this distinction matters to those who design commemorative practices.
wider: Compare Australian commemoration practices with those in Turkey, New Zealand, and France — what does each country's approach reveal about how they understand their relationship to WW1?

Investigate how ANZAC Day changed between its founding (1916) and the present — examining periods when participation declined (1950s–60s) and when it resurged (1990s–present) — and what drove each change

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat commemoration and glorification as synonymous. Making the distinction explicit — commemoration can honour sacrifice without celebrating war — is both a required endpoint outcome and conceptually important for the historiographical debate node that follows.

success_criteria: Describes the main forms of WW1 commemoration in Australia
Distinguishes commemoration from glorification with a clear explanation of what makes each different

nodes.label: Historiographical debate — how historians' views of the Anzac legend have differed over time
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss similarities and differences in historians' views of the Anzac legend over time, identifying key interpretive positions and explaining what grounds the debate.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify at least two distinct historical interpretations of the Anzac legend — e.g. the traditional celebratory view, revisionist critiques (that the legend is a myth, that it glorifies war, that it excludes women and non-Anglo Australians), and more recent inclusive expansions — and explain on what grounds historians hold different views.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the traditional legend (Bean, early official histories); the revisionist critiques from the 1970s–90s (questions about whether the legend was 'true', whether it glorified war, gender and racial exclusions); responses to revisionism (defending the legend's essential truth while acknowledging limitations); recent expansions to include First Nations soldiers, women, and multicultural contributions; explain what has changed in historians' views and what has driven the changes (new sources, new social values, new questions); explain that historians' disagreements reflect not just different evidence but different values about what the past should mean for the present.
wider: Read extracts from contrasting historians — e.g. Alistair Thomson's 'Anzac Memories', Peter Stanley's work on the legend's exclusions, or a traditional defence of the legend — and compare their claims directly, applying source analysis skills

Consider the question: is the Anzac legend a harmless national story, a positive source of values, or a dangerous myth? Develop a position and support it with historical evidence — this is an evaluative task grounded in the historiographical debate
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The evaluative position-taking task — is the legend harmless, valuable, or dangerous? — is a genuine analytical challenge where students must synthesise the whole descriptor's learning (legend content, commemoration, historiographical debate) into a supported judgement. This is the richest higher-order task the descriptor supports.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat 'historians disagree' as meaning 'nobody knows' rather than 'different evidence and different values produce different interpretations'. Making explicit what grounds a valid historical interpretation — evidence, methodology, context, values — is the scaffold for this node.

Encountering multiple distinct interpretive positions — traditional, revisionist, inclusive, evaluative — prevents students from collapsing the debate to a binary 'true or false' question about the legend.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two different historical interpretations of the Anzac legend and describes what each claims
Explains on what grounds historians hold different views — not just that they disagree, but why their interpretations differ

nodes.label: The Treaty of Versailles — fairness and consequences
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the fairness of the Treaty of Versailles on Germany, identifying its main terms and assessing the grounds on which it can be considered just or unjust.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify the main terms imposed on Germany by the Treaty of Versailles (war guilt clause, reparations, territorial losses, military restrictions), describe the German reaction to the treaty, and make a judgement about whether the treaty was fair, supported by at least one reason.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the 'Big Three' negotiating positions (Wilson's Fourteen Points, Clemenceau's punitive aims, Lloyd George's middle position); the specific terms imposed; the German delegation's exclusion from negotiations and their response (the 'diktat'); the war guilt clause (Article 231) as both legally and morally contested; the scale of reparations and territorial loss; evaluate the treaty using multiple criteria — the Allied perspective (Germany started the war and must pay), the German perspective (the terms were unprecedented and punitive), and a longer-term perspective (did the treaty's severity contribute to the conditions for WW2?); connect to the 'stab-in-the-back' myth from AC9HH9K10.
wider: Compare the Treaty of Versailles with Wilson's Fourteen Points — how much of Wilson's vision was actually implemented, and why did the final treaty diverge from it?

Evaluate the claim that the Treaty of Versailles caused WW2 — is this a defensible historical interpretation or an oversimplification? Apply the concept of turning point from AC9HH9K10 to this question
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The 'did Versailles cause WW2?' question is a genuine historiographical debate with serious scholars on multiple sides — it integrates the evaluative thinking from N3 with the turning-point concept from AC9HH9K10, producing a rich analytical extension that reaches across descriptors.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly judge the Treaty of Versailles as 'unfair' without engaging with the Allied perspective on why it was constructed as it was. Evaluating fairness requires holding multiple perspectives simultaneously — what counts as fair from each party's position — before reaching a reasoned judgement.
Examining the treaty from German, Allied, and longer-term historical perspectives builds the multiperspective understanding the evaluation task requires.

success_criteria: Identifies the main terms of the Treaty of Versailles and describes the German reaction
Evaluates the fairness of the treaty using at least two different perspectives and supports the judgement with evidence
